claim: Homeostatic signaling stabilizes synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of Drosophila, mice, and human.
source: Homeostatic signaling stabilizes synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of Drosophila, mice, and human.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established literature on homeostatic signaling across species.

claim: Homeostatic signaling at the NMJ is bi-directional.
source: It is believed that homeostatic signaling at the NMJ is bi-directional and considerable progress has been made identifying mechanisms underlying the homeostatic potentiation of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is stated as a belief in the field, supported by existing literature.

claim: Homeostatic potentiation and depression can be simultaneously induced, demonstrating true bi-directional plasticity.
source: Here, we show that homeostatic potentiation and depression can be simultaneously induced, demonstrating true bi-directional plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations that block homeostatic potentiation do not alter homeostatic depression.
source: Next, we show that mutations that block homeostatic potentiation do not alter homeostatic depression, demonstrating that these are genetically separable processes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic depression is achieved by decreased presynaptic calcium channel abundance and calcium influx.
source: Finally, we show that homeostatic depression is achieved by decreased presynaptic calcium channel abundance and calcium influx, changes that are independent of the presynaptic action potential waveform.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging and electrophysiology data in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in calcium channel abundance and calcium influx during homeostatic depression are independent of the presynaptic action potential waveform.
source: Finally, we show that homeostatic depression is achieved by decreased presynaptic calcium channel abundance and calcium influx, changes that are independent of the presynaptic action potential waveform.
evidence: This is supported by Archaerhodopsin imaging data showing no change in action potential waveform.

claim: At the Drosophila NMJ, inhibition of postsynaptic glutamate receptor function leads to a compensatory increase in presynaptic neurotransmitter release that precisely restores normal muscle depolarization.
source: At the Drosophila NMJ, inhibition of postsynaptic glutamate receptor function leads to a compensatory increase in presynaptic neurotransmitter release that precisely restores normal muscle depolarization (Petersen et al., 1997; Davis and Goodman, 1998; Davis et al., 1998; Frank et al., 2006; Davis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Presynaptic overexpression of the vesicular glutamate transporter (vGlut2) causes an increase in the amount of glutamate packaged within individual synaptic vesicles.
source: An opposing process, presynaptic homeostatic depression (PHD), can be induced by presynaptic overexpression of the vesicular glutamate transporter (vGlut2), which causes an increase in the amount of glutamate packaged within individual synaptic vesicles and a corresponding increase in synaptic vesicle diameter (Daniels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Daniels et al., 2004.

claim: Presynaptic overexpression of vGlut2 causes a corresponding increase in synaptic vesicle diameter.
source: An opposing process, presynaptic homeostatic depression (PHD), can be induced by presynaptic overexpression of the vesicular glutamate transporter (vGlut2), which causes an increase in the amount of glutamate packaged within individual synaptic vesicles and a corresponding increase in synaptic vesicle diameter (Daniels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Daniels et al., 2004.

claim: Larger vesicles produced by vGlut2 overexpression produce larger average spontaneous miniature excitatory post-synaptic potentials (mEPSPs).
source: These larger vesicles produce larger average spontaneous miniature excitatory post-synaptic potentials (mEPSPs).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A homeostatic decrease in presynaptic vesicle release maintains evoked EPSP amplitudes at wild type levels despite increased mEPSP amplitude in vGlut2 overexpressing animals.
source: A homeostatic decrease in presynaptic vesicle release, however, maintains evoked EPSP amplitudes at wild type levels despite increased mEPSP amplitude (Daniels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Animals overexpressing UAS-vGlut2 displayed a shift of the entire mEPSP amplitude distribution, corresponding to larger miniature release events.
source: Animals overexpressing UAS-vGlut2 (referred to hereafter as vGlut-OE animals) displayed a shift of the entire mEPSP amplitude distribution, corresponding to larger miniature release events (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: vGlut-OE animals have increased mEPSP amplitudes with no change in evoked EPSP amplitudes, resulting in a decrease in calculated quantal content.
source: vGlut-OE animals have increased mEPSP amplitudes (p < 0.0001) with no change in evoked EPSP amplitudes (p = 0.08), resulting in a decrease in calculated quantal content (p < 0.0001, n > 12 NMJ per genotype).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Following the induction of PHP, there is a rightward shift in the calcium cooperativity of neurotransmitter release.
source: Following the induction of PHP, there is a rightward shift in the calcium cooperativity of neurotransmitter release, indicating that the homeostatic potentiation of neurotransmitter release is robust over a range of extracellular Ca2+ concentrations and likely does not involve a change in the calcium sensor for synaptic vesicle fusion (Frank et al., 2006; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The homeostatic potentiation of neurotransmitter release is robust over a range of extracellular Ca2+ concentrations.
source: Following the induction of PHP, there is a rightward shift in the calcium cooperativity of neurotransmitter release, indicating that the homeostatic potentiation of neurotransmitter release is robust over a range of extracellular Ca2+ concentrations and likely does not involve a change in the calcium sensor for synaptic vesicle fusion (Frank et al., 2006; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PHP likely does not involve a change in the calcium sensor for synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: Following the induction of PHP, there is a rightward shift in the calcium cooperativity of neurotransmitter release, indicating that the homeostatic potentiation of neurotransmitter release is robust over a range of extracellular Ca2+ concentrations and likely does not involve a change in the calcium sensor for synaptic vesicle fusion (Frank et al., 2006; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium cooperativity data and supported by citations.

claim: PHD accurately offsets an increase in average spontaneous release event amplitude at elevated extracellular calcium (3 mM).
source: We observed that PHD accurately offset an increase in average spontaneous release event amplitude at elevated extracellular calcium (3 mM; Figure 1B,D), demonstrating that PHD proceeds accurately at extracellular calcium concentrations [Ca2+]e that span what is considered to be physiological in the intact organism (compare quantal content in Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 1B,D.

claim: PHD is robust across a range of extracellular calcium concentrations.
source: These data demonstrate that PHD is robust across a range of extracellular calcium concentrations and is likely to be independent of any change in the calcium sensor for presynaptic release.
evidence: This is supported by data showing PHD at multiple calcium concentrations.

claim: PHD is likely to be independent of any change in the calcium sensor for presynaptic release.
source: These data demonstrate that PHD is robust across a range of extracellular calcium concentrations and is likely to be independent of any change in the calcium sensor for presynaptic release.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium cooperativity data.

claim: Quantal content is able to scale across an order of magnitude in response to perturbations that increase (vGlut2 overexpression) or decrease (PhTx treatment) quantal amplitude.
source: Quantal content is able to scale across an order of magnitude in response to perturbations that increase (vGlut2 overexpression) or decrease (PhTx treatment) quantal amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PhTx application to vGlut-OE terminals significantly reduced mEPSP amplitudes in a manner quantitatively similar to that observed when PhTx is applied to wild type NMJ.
source: First, we found that PhTx application to vGlut-OE terminals significantly reduced mEPSP amplitudes in a manner quantitatively similar to that observed when PhTx is applied to wild type NMJ (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: At both wild type and vGlut-OE NMJ, the 50–60% drop in average mEPSP amplitude was offset by an approximate doubling of presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
source: At both wild type and vGlut-OE NMJ, the 50–60% drop in average mEPSP amplitude was offset by an approximate doubling of presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: EPSP amplitudes were maintained at or near wild type levels after PhTx application in both wild type and vGlut-OE NMJ.
source: As a result, in both wild type and vGlut-OE NMJ, EPSP amplitudes were maintained at or near wild type levels after PhTx application (a slight decrease in EPSP amplitude was observed in vGlut-OE animals, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: There was no difference in EPSP amplitude comparing wild type (+PhTx) and vGlut-OE (+PhTx).
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in EPSP amplitude comparing wild type (+PhTx) and vGlut-OE (+PhTx; p > 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiology data.

claim: Despite vGlut-OE NMJ chronically expressing PHD during larval development, application of PhTx is able to induce expression of PHP that appears unaffected by prior induction of PHD.
source: Thus, despite the fact that vGlut-OE NMJ chronically express PHD during larval development, application of PhTx is able to induce expression of PHP that appears unaffected by prior induction of PHD.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing normal PHP in vGlut-OE animals treated with PhTx.

claim: The mechanisms of PHP and PHD can co-exist at a single NMJ and can be sequentially induced.
source: First, these data demonstrate that the mechanisms of PHP and PHD can co-exist at a single NMJ and can be sequentially induced, at least in the sequence that we performed in this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing both PHP and PHD at the same NMJ.

claim: The reduced presynaptic release caused by vGlut2 overexpression is not a secondary effect whereby vGlut2 overabundance disrupts the vesicle fusion apparatus.
source: Second, the data argue that the reduced presynaptic release caused by vGlut2 overexpression is not a secondary effect whereby vGlut2 overabundance disrupts the vesicle fusion apparatus, since release can be precisely potentiated at this NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability to induce PHP in vGlut-OE animals.

claim: The mechanisms of PHP and PHD can be effectively combined to fine tune presynaptic release.
source: Finally, these data demonstrate that the mechanisms of PHP and PHD can be effectively combined to fine tune presynaptic release.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing accurate homeostatic compensation when both PHP and PHD are induced.

claim: The potentiation of neurotransmitter release during PHP requires a presynaptic ENaC channel.
source: It was recently demonstrated that the potentiation of neurotransmitter release during PHP requires a presynaptic ENaC channel (Younger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of the presynaptic ENaC channel, or genetic mutation of the gene encoding an essential subunit of this channel, eliminates the expression of homeostatic potentiation.
source: Briefly, in either a glutamate receptor mutant background, or following acute application of PhTx to the NMJ, subsequent pharmacological inhibition of the presynaptic ENaC channel, or genetic mutation of the gene encoding an essential subunit of this channel, eliminates the expression of homeostatic potentiation (Younger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ENaC channels do not appear to be present on the membrane under baseline conditions.
source: Importantly, ENaC channels do not appear to be present on the membrane under baseline conditions since deletion or pharmacological blockade of these channels does not decrease baseline neurotransmitter release (Younger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Application of the ENaC channel inhibitor benzamil (25 µM) had no significant effect on presynaptic release at vGlut-OE NMJ.
source: We found no significant effect of benzamil on presynaptic release at vGlut-OE NMJ, consistent with the expectation that ENaC channels do not participate in baseline release in wild type animals and, therefore, cannot be removed as a mechanism underlying PHD. (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Application of Benzamil prevents PHP expression in the vGlut-OE background.
source: As a control, we tested whether application of Benzamil still prevents PHP expression in the vGlut-OE background. We found that this is, indeed, the case (vGlut-OE +Benzamil: mEPSP = 0.83 ± 0.05 mV, QC = 39.2 ± 2.3; vGlut-OE +Benzamil +PhTx: mEPSP = 0.50 ± 0.02 mV, QC = 43.6 ± 3.0; quantal content is statistically unchanged; p = 0.29, n > 10).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for PHD are molecularly separable from those that drive PHP.
source: Taken together, these data imply that the mechanisms responsible for PHD are molecularly separable from those that drive PHP.
evidence: This is inferred from the benzamil experiments showing no effect on PHD.

claim: Multiple loss of function alleles of the rim gene, including a deletion that removes a large portion of the coding sequence (rim103), all block PHP.
source: We previously demonstrated that multiple loss of function alleles of the rim gene, including a deletion that removes a large portion of the coding sequence (rim103), all block PHP, independent of whether they also impair baseline presynaptic release (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: vGlut2 overexpression in the rim103 mutant background still induced robust expression of PHD.
source: By contrast, vGlut2 overexpression in the rim103 mutant background still induced robust expression of PHD (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: RIM is not required for PHD.
source: These data demonstrate that RIM is not required for PHD and further separate the mechanisms that promote PHD vs PHP.
evidence: This is inferred from the rim103 mutant data showing normal PHD.

claim: The cacS mutation is a single amino acid substitution in the sixth transmembrane domain of the third repeat of the pore forming subunit of the CaV2.1 channel.
source: The cacS mutation is a single amino acid substitution in the sixth transmembrane domain of the third repeat of the pore forming subunit of the CaV2.1 channel (Brooks et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cacS mutation prevents low-voltage modulation of CaV2.1 calcium channels following insertion of ENaC channels in the presynaptic membrane.
source: In a current model of PHP, the cacS mutation prevents low-voltage modulation of CaV2.1 calcium channels following insertion of ENaC channels in the presynaptic membrane (Younger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cacS mutation causes a ∼30% decrease in presynaptic calcium influx and a corresponding decrease in presynaptic release at baseline.
source: Because the cacS mutation causes a ∼30% decrease in presynaptic calcium influx and a corresponding decrease in presynaptic release at baseline (Müller and Davis, 2012), we performed our analysis at elevated (1 mM) extracellular calcium.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Although the cacS mutation completely blocks PHP, it had no effect on PHD at vGlut-OE NMJ.
source: Although the cacS mutation completely blocks PHP, we observed no effect on PHD at vGlut-OE NMJ (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying PHD are distinct from those that drive PHP.
source: Taken together with the observation that PHD is insensitive to benzamil treatment and occurs normally in the presence of a RIM deletion, our data demonstrate that the molecular mechanisms underlying PHD are distinct from those that drive PHP.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple genetic experiments showing separation of PHP and PHD mechanisms.

claim: The expression of PHP is achieved, in part, by an increase in presynaptic calcium influx through CaV2.1 calcium channels.
source: The expression of PHP is achieved, in part, by an increase in presynaptic calcium influx through CaV2.1 calcium channels (Frank et al., 2006; Müller and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Archaerhodopsin can be expressed in motoneurons without affecting baseline neurotransmission.
source: However, it was recently demonstrated that Archaerhodopsin can be expressed in motoneurons without affecting baseline neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The voltage sensitive properties of Archaerhodopsin can be used to visualize the presynaptic action potential waveform with high temporal resolution.
source: The voltage sensitive properties of Archaerhodopsin can be used to visualize the presynaptic action potential waveform with high temporal resolution (Ford and Davis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Archaerhodopsin imaging has sufficient temporal resolution to quantify changes in action potential half-width that correlate with either a 50% increase or decrease in neurotransmitter release.
source: Importantly, this technique has sufficient temporal resolution to quantify changes in action potential half-width that correlate with either a 50% increase or decrease in neurotransmitter release (Ford and Davis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The induction of PHP following application of PhTx to the NMJ or in animals containing a mutation in the muscle specific glutamate receptor GluRIIA did not cause an increase in AP width or WHM.
source: Using Arch-GFP to image the presynaptic AP waveform, we observed that the induction of PHP following application of PhTx to the NMJ or in animals containing a mutation in the muscle specific glutamate receptor GluRIIA did not cause an increase in AP width or WHM (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Archaerhodopsin imaging data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: There was no change in AP waveform comparing wild type with vGlut-OE animals.
source: In both cases, there was no change in AP waveform comparing wild type with vGlut-OE animals (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Archaerhodopsin imaging data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Both PHP and PHD occur normally in the presence of Arch-GFP.
source: We also controlled for the possibility that Arch-GFP imaging might alter the expression of PHP or PHD by recording neuromuscular transmission from the same genotypes in which we quantified AP waveforms. We found that both PHP, using either PhTx or the GluRIIA mutation, and PHD occur normally in the presence of Arch-GFP (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The homeostatic modulation of presynaptic neurotransmitter release, either PHP or PHD, is not correlated with a change in AP waveform measured at the presynaptic nerve terminal.
source: From these data, we conclude that the homeostatic modulation of presynaptic neurotransmitter release, either PHP or PHD, is not correlated with a change in AP waveform measured at the presynaptic nerve terminal.
evidence: This is inferred from the Archaerhodopsin imaging data.

claim: PHP requires two parallel changes within the presynaptic nerve terminal: (1) an increase in calcium influx through CaV2.1 calcium channels and (2) an increase in the RRP.
source: PHP requires two parallel changes within the presynaptic nerve terminal; (1) an increase in calcium influx through CaV2.1 calcium channels and (2) an increase in the RRP.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and established knowledge.

claim: The RRP was not significantly different when comparing wild type and vGlut-OE animals.
source: We found that the RRP was not significantly different when comparing wild type and vGlut-OE animals (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Homeostatic depression is not correlated with a drop in the size of the RRP.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that homeostatic depression is not correlated with a drop in the size of the RRP, highlighting a mechanistic difference in the expression of PHP and PHD.
evidence: This is inferred from the RRP measurements in vGlut-OE animals.

claim: Ptrain was significantly lower in vGlut-OE animals as compared to wild type, indicating reduced presynaptic release probability.
source: Using this method, we found Ptrain to be significantly lower in vGlut-OE animals as compared to wild type, indicating reduced presynaptic release probability (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5C.

claim: vGlut-OE is associated with a decrease in presynaptic release probability.
source: We conclude that vGlut-OE is associated with a decrease in presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This is inferred from the Ptrain measurements.

claim: There was a ∼50% reduction in calcium influx in vGlut-OE animals compared to wild type following single action potential stimulation.
source: Following single action potential stimulation, we observed a ∼50% reduction in calcium influx in vGlut-OE animals compared to wild type (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 6A-C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the basal calcium signal between wild type and vGlut-OE animals.
source: There was no significant difference in the basal calcium signal, indicating that this effect was not caused by differences in dye loading (Figure 6C, left).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 6C.

claim: PHD is correlated with a large decrease in presynaptic calcium influx.
source: These data indicate that PHD is correlated with a large decrease in presynaptic calcium influx and suggests that this is a primary mechanism driving the process.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data.

claim: Overexpression of CaV2.1-GFP does not influence baseline neurotransmission.
source: Overexpression of CaV2.1-GFP does not influence baseline neurotransmission and serves as a reliable reporter of active-zone localized presynaptic channels (Kawasaki et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Overexpressed CaV2.1-GFP can report changes in presynaptic calcium channel abundance.
source: Previous reports demonstrate that overexpressed CaV2.1-GFP can report changes in presynaptic calcium channel abundance (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of CaV2.1-GFP did not affect PHD induction in vGlut-OE animals.
source: Consistent with prior reports, we found that overexpression of CaV2.1-GFP did not affect transmission in wild type animals and, furthermore, did not affect PHD induction in vGlut-OE animals (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: There was a 30% and 50% decrease in CaV2.1-GFP signal at type 1B and type 1S boutons, respectively, in vGlut-OE animals compared to wild type.
source: Strikingly, we observed a 30% and 50% decrease in CaV2.1-GFP signal at type 1B and type 1S boutons, respectively, in vGlut-OE animals compared to wild type (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 7E-H.

claim: There was no change in the levels of Brp in vGlut-OE animals compared to wild type.
source: There was no change in the levels of Brp, assayed by measurement of anti-BRP fluorescence intensity (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 7E-H.

claim: The number of Brp puncta per bouton was not significantly changed in vGlut-OE animals.
source: We also quantified the number of Brp puncta per bouton as an estimate of active zone number per bouton and found no significant change (vGlut-OE: 12.1 ± 2.0 and 6.4 ± 1.4 puncta per type 1B and 1S bouton, respectively, N = 11 NMJ; WT: 13.3 ± 1.5 and 7.5 ± 2.1. p > 0.05 for both, N = 12 NMJ).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of imaging data.

claim: The observed decrease in CaV2.1-GFP signal is not a secondary consequence of grossly altered active zone organization.
source: These data indicate that the observed decrease in CaV2.1-GFP signal is not a secondary consequence of grossly altered active zone organization, consistent with previous electron microscopic analysis of the vGlut-OE NMJ (Daniels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the Brp data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CaV2.1 levels are not modulated at the level of transcription during PHD.
source: Since UAS-CaV2.1-GFP expression is independent of the normal transcriptional regulation of the CaV2.1 gene locus, these data additionally suggest that CaV2.1 levels are not modulated at the level of transcription during PHD, but rather that CaV2.1 protein is selectively restricted from entering the active zone or is selectively removed from the active zone.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of a transgenic CaV2.1-GFP construct.

claim: Reduced presynaptic CaV2.1 abundance underlies the decreased neurotransmitter release observed during homeostatic depression.
source: We conclude that reduced presynaptic CaV2.1 abundance underlies the decreased neurotransmitter release observed during homeostatic depression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined calcium imaging and CaV2.1-GFP imaging data.

claim: PHD is driven by a reduction in presynaptic calcium channel abundance at individual active zones.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PHD is driven by a reduction in presynaptic calcium channel abundance at individual active zones.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by imaging data.

claim: This mechanism is consistent with the co-expression and co-regulation of PHD and PHP, achieving bi-directional homeostatic control of neurotransmission at the NMJ.
source: This mechanism is consistent with the co-expression and co-regulation of PHD and PHP, achieving bi-directional homeostatic control of neurotransmission at the NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on PHP and PHD mechanisms.

claim: PHP is driven by the regulated insertion of an ENaC channel in the presynaptic membrane.
source: More specifically, recent data support a model in which PHP is driven by the regulated insertion of an ENaC channel in the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and established knowledge.

claim: ENaC channel insertion is thought to cause a modest depolarization of the presynaptic membrane, subsequent potentiation of calcium influx and enhanced vesicle release.
source: This is thought to cause a modest depolarization of the presynaptic membrane, subsequent potentiation of calcium influx and enhanced vesicle release (Davis, 2013; Younger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If PHD is driven by a decrease in calcium channel number, PHP can be subsequently induced through insertion of presynaptic ENaC channels.
source: Therefore, if PHD is driven by a decrease in calcium channel number, PHP can be subsequently induced through insertion of presynaptic ENaC channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanisms of PHP and PHD.

claim: Application of an ENaC channel blocker prevents expression of PHP in the vGlut-OE background.
source: Consistent with this idea, application of an ENaC channel blocker prevents expression of PHP in the vGlut-OE background.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: PHP and PHD can be combined to precisely target the correct EPSP amplitude, offsetting two persistent perturbations: enlarged presynaptic vesicles, and impaired postsynaptic glutamate receptor sensitivity.
source: Although the proposed mechanisms of PHP and PHD are compatible, it is none-the-less remarkable that PHP and PHD can be combined to precisely target the correct EPSP amplitude, offsetting two persistent perturbations: enlarged presynaptic vesicles, and impaired postsynaptic glutamate receptor sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing accurate compensation.

claim: The genetic underpinnings responsible for PHP and PHD are distinct.
source: Our data indicate that the genetic underpinnings responsible for PHP and PHD are distinct, since three conditions that block PHP have no impact on PHD.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments.

claim: Rheostat-like modulation of presynaptic release is achieved by the intersection of two distinct signaling systems driving PHP and PHD.
source: Thus, we propose that rheostat-like modulation of presynaptic release is achieved by the intersection of two distinct signaling systems driving PHP and PHD.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Auxiliary calcium channel subunits such as α2δ have mutant phenotypes that affect presynaptic calcium influx and calcium channel abundance.
source: Although auxiliary calcium channel subunits such as α2δ have mutant phenotypes that affect presynaptic calcium influx and calcium channel abundance (Dickman et al., 2008; Ly et al., 2008; Hoppa et al., 2012), it remains unknown whether these auxiliary subunits acutely modulate calcium channel abundance in response to activity, as opposed to simply establishing and maintaining baseline expression levels during development and throughout the life of a synapse.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The magnitude of the decrease in calcium channel abundance and presynaptic calcium influx should cause a much larger decrease in quantal content than what is observed during PHD.
source: Even though our measurements of calcium channel number and calcium influx are internally consistent, and our measurements of quantal content during PHD corroborate prior publications, there remains a discrepancy. The magnitude of the decrease in calcium channel abundance and presynaptic calcium influx should cause a much larger decrease in quantal content that what we observe during PHD.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of calcium measurements and quantal content.

claim: The relationship between release and external calcium is a power function with an exponent of approximately three at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: More specifically, the relationship between release and external calcium is a power function with an exponent of approximately three at the Drosophila NMJ (Dickman and Davis, 2009; Müller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A 50% drop in the spatially averaged calcium signal should decrease release by more than the observed 30%.
source: Therefore, a 50% drop in the spatially averaged calcium signal should decrease release by more than the observed 30%.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium cooperativity relationship.

claim: There is a linear relationship between the RRP and extracellular calcium at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: We recently documented a linear relationship between the RRP and extracellular calcium at this synapse (Müller et al., 2015), consistent with similar observations at the mammalian calyx of held (Thanawala and Regehr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms of PHD may include two inter-dependent processes: a drop in calcium channel abundance and a mechanism that potentiates the RRP to achieve precise homeostatic compensation.
source: One possibility, therefore, is that the mechanisms of PHD include two inter-dependent processes. First, there is a drop in calcium channel abundance. Second, there is a mechanism that potentiates the RRP to achieve precise homeostatic compensation.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the discrepancy.

claim: Increasing vesicular size may directly increase Pr at hippocampal synapses.
source: Alternatively, recent evidence indicates that increasing vesicular size may directly increase Pr at hippocampal synapses (Herman et al., 2014), suggesting another model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The overexpression of vGlut2, which causes increased vesicle diameter, would cause a concomitant increase in Pr.
source: In this model, the overexpression of vGlut2, which causes increased vesicle diameter (Daniels et al., 2004), would cause a concomitant increase in Pr.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on prior work.

claim: Application of PhTx to vGlut-OE animals results in an NMJ that releases enlarged vesicles, but with resulting mEPSPs that are smaller than normal.
source: Application of PhTx to vGlut-OE animals results in an NMJ that releases enlarged vesicles, but with resulting mEPSPs that are smaller than normal.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: In the presence of both perturbations (vGlut-OE and PhTx), the homeostatic signaling system is able to restore EPSP amplitudes to precisely wild type levels.
source: In the presence of both perturbations, the homeostatic signaling system is able to restore EPSP amplitudes to precisely wild type levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PhTx induces homeostatic potentiation in 10 min.
source: Because PhTx induces homeostatic potentiation in 10 min, and because there does not appear to be a reservoir of CaV2.1 channels present extra-synaptically in vGlut-OE animals, it is unlikely that there is sufficient time to repopulate all of the active zones at the NMJ with calcium channels, thereby erasing PHD and allowing the system to function solely according to PHP.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge and inference from the data.

claim: The correct restoration of EPSP amplitude likely occurs through the summation of PHP and PHD.
source: Thus, the correct restoration of EPSP amplitude likely occurs through the summation of PHP and PHD.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Both PHP and PHD presumably require retrograde signaling from the muscle to the motor neuron to drive the observed changes in presynaptic release.
source: Both PHP and PHD presumably require retrograde signaling from the muscle to the motor neuron to drive the observed changes in presynaptic release.
